```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
has_arimatools <- requireNamespace("arimatools", quietly = TRUE)
```

This vignette is the R version of the demonstration notebook of the Python
package Forecasting-Tools. It simulates an ARMA(1,1), estimates a correctly
specified ARMA(1,1) and a misspecified AR(1), produces static forecasts for
an evaluation sample, and evaluates and compares them:

| Step | Functions |
|:--|:--|
| Static forecasting | `static_forecast()` |
| Accuracy | `me()`, `mae()`, `mse()`, `rmse()`, `mape()`, `forecast_accuracy()` |
| Diagnostics of each forecast | `unbiasedness_test()`, `weak_efficiency_test()`, `orthogonality_test()` |
| Comparison of two forecasts | `mgn_test()`, `dm_test()`, `encompassing_test()` |

Forecast errors are always **actual minus forecast**. The numbers differ from
those of the Python notebook, because R and NumPy generate different random
numbers; given the same data, both packages give the same results.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(forecastingtools)
library(forecast)
```

## 1. Simulated data and estimation

The data-generating process is
$y_t - \mu = \phi (y_{t-1} - \mu) + \varepsilon_t + \theta \varepsilon_{t-1}$
with $\phi = 0.7$, $\theta = 0.4$, $\mu = 100$ and $\sigma = 2$. After a
burn-in of 500 observations we keep 300: the first 250 for estimation, the
last 50 for evaluation.

```{r}
set.seed(20261008)
y <- ts(100 + arima.sim(list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.4), n = 300, sd = 2, n.start = 500))
estimation <- window(y, end = 250)
actual <- window(y, start = 251)

models <- list(
  "ARMA(1,1)" = Arima(estimation, order = c(1, 0, 1)),
  "AR(1)"     = Arima(estimation, order = c(1, 0, 0))
)
lapply(models, coef)
```

For stationary models, `intercept` is the mean $\mu$, not the constant of the
recursion. The correctly specified model need not beat the simpler one in a
finite sample.

## 2. Static forecasting

A **static** (sequential one-step) forecast keeps the estimated parameters
fixed and, for each evaluation period,

1. forecasts the next observation with the information available,
2. observes the actual value, and
3. adds it to the information set before the next forecast.

Each actual value is used only after its own forecast. A **dynamic** forecast,
by contrast, is issued once at the end of the estimation sample and never uses
later observations.

```{r}
forecasts <- lapply(models, static_forecast, actual = actual, level = 0.95)
head(forecasts[["ARMA(1,1)"]], 4)
```

The intervals are conditional Gaussian prediction intervals: they ignore the
uncertainty of the estimated parameters. The first static forecast is the
one-step dynamic forecast; afterwards the two differ.

```{r}
stopifnot(
  all.equal(forecasts[["ARMA(1,1)"]]$forecast[1],
            as.numeric(forecast(models[["ARMA(1,1)"]], h = 1)$mean)),
  all.equal(forecasts[["ARMA(1,1)"]]$error,
            as.numeric(actual) - forecasts[["ARMA(1,1)"]]$forecast)
)
```

```{r, fig.cap = "Static one-step forecasts, with the 95% interval of the ARMA(1,1)."}
arma <- forecasts[["ARMA(1,1)"]]; ar <- forecasts[["AR(1)"]]
plot(arma$time, arma$actual, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = range(arma$lower, arma$upper),
     xlab = "Evaluation period", ylab = "y")
polygon(c(arma$time, rev(arma$time)), c(arma$lower, rev(arma$upper)),
        col = adjustcolor("steelblue", 0.15), border = NA)
lines(arma$time, arma$forecast, col = "steelblue", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
lines(ar$time, ar$forecast, col = "darkorange", lty = 3, lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Actual", "ARMA(1,1)", "AR(1)"), lty = 1:3,
       col = c("black", "steelblue", "darkorange"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

## 3. Forecast accuracy

With $e_t = y_t - \hat y_t$ and $n = 50$,
$\mathrm{ME} = \frac1n \sum e_t$, $\mathrm{MAE} = \frac1n \sum |e_t|$,
$\mathrm{MSE} = \frac1n \sum e_t^2$, $\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}}$ and
$\mathrm{MAPE} = \frac{100}{n} \sum |e_t / y_t|$.

```{r}
accuracy <- sapply(forecasts, function(f) forecast_accuracy(f$actual, f$forecast))
round(accuracy, 4)
```

ME measures bias (positive: underforecasting), and positive and negative errors
cancel; the other measures describe the size of the errors. MSE and RMSE
always rank models in the same way. A lower RMSE is a realized outcome in this
sample, not evidence that one model is better: that is what the tests in
Sections 5 to 7 address.

## 4. Diagnostics of each forecast

### Unbiasedness

The **mean-error test** estimates $e_t = a + u_t$ and tests $H_0: a = 0$. The
**Mincer-Zarnowitz test** estimates $y_t = a + b \hat y_t + u_t$ and tests
$H_0: a = 0, b = 1$ jointly. Inference is HAC (Newey-West, Bartlett weights,
automatic bandwidth, no small-sample adjustment) by default.

```{r}
unbiasedness_test(actual, arma$forecast)
sapply(forecasts, function(f) {
  r <- unbiasedness_test(actual, f$forecast, method = "mincer_zarnowitz")
  c(intercept = r$coefficients$estimate[1], slope = r$coefficients$estimate[2],
    chi2 = r$statistic, p.value = r$p.value)
})
```

### Weak efficiency

Optimal one-step errors are serially uncorrelated. With `h = 1`,
`weak_efficiency_test()` applies the Ljung-Box test to the errors; it does
not test bias, because the errors are centered.

```{r}
sapply(forecasts, function(f) {
  r <- weak_efficiency_test(actual, f$forecast, h = 1, lags = 10)
  c(Q = r$statistic, df = r$df, p.value = r$p.value)
})
```

### Orthogonality

The last observed value $y_{t-1}$ is known when $y_t$ is forecast. We build it
from the complete series, so the first evaluation row uses the last estimation
observation. The function never shifts or aligns the information itself.

```{r}
previous <- as.numeric(y)[250:299]          # y_{t-1} for t = 251, ..., 300
stopifnot(previous[1] == estimation[250])
r <- orthogonality_test(actual, arma$forecast, cbind(previous = previous))
r
```

For the AR(1), the forecast is an affine function of $y_{t-1}$, so its
Mincer-Zarnowitz and orthogonality regressions span the same information and
give the same statistic: they are not independent confirmations.

```{r}
c(MZ = unbiasedness_test(actual, ar$forecast, "mincer_zarnowitz")$statistic,
  orthogonality = orthogonality_test(actual, ar$forecast, previous)$statistic)
```

## 5. Morgan-Granger-Newbold

With $u_t = e_{1t} + e_{2t}$ and $v_t = e_{1t} - e_{2t}$, the MGN test
regresses $u_t$ on $v_t$ and tests a zero slope:
$\mathrm{Cov}(u, v) = \mathrm{Var}(e_1) - \mathrm{Var}(e_2) = 0$. Only if both
errors have zero population means is this equal MSFE.

```{r}
mgn <- mgn_test(actual, arma$forecast, ar$forecast)
mgn
mgn_c <- mgn_test(actual, arma$forecast, ar$forecast, cov_type = "nonrobust")
# The conventional version is the classical correlation statistic
stopifnot(all.equal(mgn_c$statistic,
                    mgn_c$correlation * sqrt(48 / (1 - mgn_c$correlation^2))))
```

## 6. Diebold-Mariano

With the loss differential $d_t = L(e_{1t}) - L(e_{2t})$, the DM test tests
$H_0: E(d_t) = 0$ directly, without assuming zero-mean errors. Negative mean
differentials favour model 1 (ARMA).

```{r}
sapply(c("squared", "absolute"), function(loss) {
  r <- dm_test(actual, arma$forecast, ar$forecast, loss = loss)
  c(mean_loss_diff = r$mean_loss_diff, DM = r$statistic, p.value = r$p.value)
})
```

### The DM test is a HAC regression on a constant

`dm_test()` computes $\bar d / \sqrt{\hat\Omega / n}$ directly. This is
exactly the HAC t statistic of the regression of $d_t$ on a constant, with the
same Bartlett bandwidth and no small-sample adjustment. The check below
estimates that regression with `lm()` and `sandwich::NeweyWest()`.

```{r}
dm <- dm_test(actual, arma$forecast, ar$forecast)
d <- (actual - arma$forecast)^2 - (actual - ar$forecast)^2
reg <- lm(d ~ 1)
V <- sandwich::NeweyWest(reg, lag = dm$maxlags, prewhite = FALSE, adjust = FALSE)
comparison <- rbind(
  "Direct DM"      = c(dm$mean_loss_diff, dm$se, dm$dm_statistic, dm$p.value),
  "HAC regression" = c(coef(reg), sqrt(V[1, 1]), coef(reg) / sqrt(V[1, 1]),
                       2 * pnorm(-abs(coef(reg) / sqrt(V[1, 1])))))
colnames(comparison) <- c("mean", "se", "statistic", "p.value")
comparison
stopifnot(max(abs(comparison[1, ] - comparison[2, ])) < 1e-12)
```

`prewhite = FALSE` and `adjust = FALSE` are needed: by default
`NeweyWest()` prewhitens and applies a small-sample factor.

### Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction

The HLN correction multiplies the statistic by
$\sqrt{(n + 1 - 2h + h(h-1)/n)/n}$ and uses a Student t(n - 1).

```{r}
hln <- dm_test(actual, arma$forecast, ar$forecast, hln = TRUE)
c(DM = dm$statistic, HLN = hln$statistic, p_DM = dm$p.value, p_HLN = hln$p.value)
```

## 7. Forecast encompassing

Does one forecast contain all the useful information of the other? With
$d_t = \hat y_{1t} - \hat y_{2t}$, the difference regression $e_{1t} = \beta d_t
+ u_t$ tests whether ARMA(1,1) encompasses AR(1), and $e_{2t} = \beta d_t +
u_t$ the reverse. The two directions are separate hypotheses.

```{r}
grid <- expand.grid(method = c("difference", "cross_forecast", "unrestricted"),
                    direction = c("1_encompasses_2", "2_encompasses_1"),
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
grid$statistic <- NA_real_
grid$p.value <- NA_real_
for (i in seq_len(nrow(grid))) {
  r <- encompassing_test(actual, arma$forecast, ar$forecast,
                         method = grid$method[i], direction = grid$direction[i])
  grid$statistic[i] <- r$statistic; grid$p.value[i] <- r$p.value
}
grid
```

Not rejecting a direction means the restriction cannot be rejected, not that
it holds; rejecting it does not mean the competing forecast is more accurate.

## 8. Models with interventions

A model estimated with intervention regressors (additive outliers, level
shifts, temporary changes) can be evaluated by static forecasting too, because
the future path of each intervention is known: an AO is 0, an LS stays at 1
and a TC keeps decaying. `arimatools::extend_interventions()` generates these
values.

```{r, eval = has_arimatools}
set.seed(2)
z <- ts(cumsum(rnorm(140)), start = c(1990, 1), frequency = 4)
z[60:140] <- z[60:140] + 5                   # level shift in 2004Q4
z_est <- window(z, end = c(2014, 4))
z_eva <- window(z, start = c(2015, 1))
X <- arimatools::outlier_regressors(z_est, dates = "2004Q4", types = "LS")
fit_ls <- Arima(z_est, order = c(1, 1, 0), xreg = X)
fit_no <- Arima(z_est, order = c(1, 1, 0))
sf_ls <- static_forecast(fit_ls, z_eva, xreg = arimatools::extend_interventions(X, 40))
sf_no <- static_forecast(fit_no, z_eva)
dm_test(z_eva, sf_ls$forecast, sf_no$forecast)
```

Interventions detected in the *evaluation* period cannot be added this way:
that would use information from after the forecast origins, and
`static_forecast()` rejects intervention values that contradict their
definition.

For other regressors, a static forecast of $y_t$ uses $x_t$. If $x_t$ is not
known at the forecast origin, the result is a conditional (ex post) forecast,
which overstates real-time accuracy; `static_forecast()` then prints a message
and marks the result with `attr(, "conditional") = TRUE`.
